title: Correcting in Green Pen Does Not Work
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton follows his earlier controversial post on copying things down with an observational test of green-pen corrections. In schools whose retrieval Do Nows repeat the same topic through a week, he follows individual students who made a green-pen correction on Monday and shows they still get a similar question wrong later, across five examples from five schools. His explanation is that corrections are passive, require no thinking, and give the appearance of learning to students, teachers and senior leaders alike. The alternative is Book-to-Board, where students show their final answers on mini-whiteboards, followed by model, check for listening and recheck for understanding with a pre-planned follow-up question. He is open about the limits (small examples, a fallback to green pen if leaders demand evidence in books), and the argument is clear and evidence-based.
points: The belief that corrections in green pen fix errors is tested using repeated Do Now questions, and in five cases from five schools the students still failed the later question.
Corrections persist because everyone benefits: students avoid thinking, teachers see silent compliance, and leaders see 'evidence' in books.
Correcting is passive and masks the lack of thinking, creating the appearance that learning has occurred.
Book-to-Board lets the teacher see all students' answers, and the response sequence is model, check for listening, then recheck understanding.
The follow-up question is the only real evidence an explanation worked, and if it fails the concept needs lesson time later, not a repeat on tomorrow's Do Now.
quotes: The most controversial newsletter I have written recently is the Myth of Copying Things Down. In that post, I argued that not only is asking students to copy notes and corrections largely a waste of precious lesson time, but it could also be detrimental to learning.

Everyone is happy with this arrangement. The students are happy because copying a correction in green pen requires no thinking. Teachers are happy because a sea of students silently correcting work can be construed as an indication that their explanation has made sense.

But, my objections aside, here we have a good way of testing the effectiveness of green pen corrections. Because, if a student struggles with a particular topic on Monday, but then does their green pen correction, then they should be able to get the question on that topic correct when it comes up again later that week.

In each of these examples, the students have done exactly what they have been told to do: make corrections in green pen. But in each instance, that correction has not led to any improvement in learning.

I alluded to the reason at the top of the post: green pen corrections are easy. Correcting is a passive activity. Correcting is something you can do without thinking. Crucially, correcting also masks this lack of thinking because it gives the appearance that thinking and learning have occurred.

In maths, a mini-whiteboard is a Godsend. Students can still answer the questions on a sheet or in their books, but when it is time to go through the answers, they copy their final answer to any given question nice and big on their board and hold it up for the teacher to see when instructed.

If we move on, there is little point in including the question on tomorrow’s Do Now. Instead, we need to free up lesson time in the future to address the concept properly. If students nail the follow-up question, then it is still useful to include a similar question in a subsequent Do Now to ensure we separate performance in the moment from longer-term learning.
